claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed ambient oxide layer before exposure.
The native oxide scale governs Q235 corrosion performance under room-temperature conditions.
The native oxide scale governs Q235 corrosion performance under high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealing can reorganize the native oxide scale on Q235 steel.
Annealing promotes more coherent, adherent, and protective iron-oxide phases on Q235 steel.
More coherent and adherent iron-oxide phases resist spallation caused by thermal-expansion and salt-induced stresses.
Untreated native oxides develop brittle phases that crack and spall.
Cracking and spallation of untreated oxides accelerate corrosion.
Annealing-induced restructuring of the native scale reduces spallation and mass loss during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
Annealed Q235 will have a more uniform and adherent oxide layer than untreated Q235 after high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 will exhibit lower mass change and reduced degradation than untreated Q235 under high-temperature salt exposure.
At room temperature, annealed and untreated Q235 will show similar short-term passivation behavior.
The proposed annealing concept is analogous to improved oxide structure observed in atmospheric plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy coatings on SS316L.
The proposed mechanism should not apply below the salt or temperature thresholds that drive oxide phase transformations.
The mechanism is expected to dominate in low-alloy steels whose native oxide is primarily iron-based.
Additional alloying elements or non-native protective coatings may independently alter oxide formation and adhesion, limiting applicability of the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the native oxide governs corrosion performance under both room- and high-temperature salt conditions, while the conditions state that the mechanism should not apply below thresholds for oxide transformations; the room-temperature prediction also expects no meaningful treatment-dependent difference.
